Description: Fingerstick readings or a continuous sensor stream. One metric, two very different data shapes. (Self Reported)
Percentage saturation, spot-checked or sampled through the night.
Systolic and diastolic from a cuff, usually logged together with the pulse. Orthostatic pairs matter for some conditions.
A recorded waveform plus the rhythm classification derived from it. Stored as a file, not a number.
Beats per minute at rest, in activity or overnight. The most commonly synced measure and the one most apps lead with.
Breaths per minute, generally derived overnight by a wearable rather than measured directly.
Phase and flow. Not behaviour, but a daily log without a clinical band, so the axis places it here.
Total CO2 in blood, mostly bicarbonate. The main buffer for acid-base balance.
Total blood calcium. Reflects bone, parathyroid and vitamin D status and affects muscles and nerves.
Electrolyte that moves with sodium and helps balance fluids and acid-base status.
Serum magnesium level. Supports nerve, muscle and heart rhythm function and can drop with diarrhoea or certain medications.
Mineral tied to bone and energy metabolism. Interacts with calcium, vitamin D and kidney function.
Key electrolyte for heart and muscle rhythm. Both high and low levels need attention.
Main electrolyte controlling water balance. Shifts with hydration, fluid losses and some medications.
Enzyme from the pancreas and salivary glands. Raised in pancreatitis and some other abdominal conditions.
Enzyme released from muscle. Rises with muscle injury, intense exercise or some medications.
Enzyme found in nearly all tissues. A non-specific marker of cell damage or red cell breakdown.
Pancreatic enzyme. Raised markedly in acute pancreatitis.
Enzyme from bile ducts and bone. Raised with bile flow problems and some bone conditions.
Liver enzyme, the most liver-specific of the transaminases. Rises with liver cell injury.
Enzyme found in liver, heart and muscle. Read alongside ALT to assess liver injury.
Liver and bile duct enzyme. Helps tell whether a raised ALP comes from the liver.
Breakdown product of red cells, processed by the liver. Raised in liver or bile duct problems and with red cell breakdown.
Blood glucose after at least 8 hours without food. Used to screen for and monitor diabetes.
Average blood glucose over roughly the past three months. The standard long-term marker of glucose control.
Main blood protein made by the liver. Reflects nutrition, liver function and protein loss.
Sum of albumin and globulins in blood. A broad indicator of nutrition, liver and immune status.
Muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys. Used to estimate kidney function.
Estimated kidney filtration rate, calculated from creatinine, age and sex. The main overall measure of kidney function.
Waste product of protein breakdown, cleared by the kidneys. Reflects kidney function and hydration.
End product of purine metabolism. High levels relate to gout and kidney stones.
Heart muscle protein released with cardiac injury. The key blood test for a heart attack.
Clotting time for the intrinsic pathway. Used to monitor heparin and to look for clotting factor problems.
Fragment released when a clot breaks down. Used mainly to rule out blood clots when the result is normal.
Clotting protein made by the liver. Also rises with inflammation.
Blood clotting time, with INR as its standardised ratio. Used to monitor warfarin and to assess clotting and liver function.
Stress hormone from the adrenal glands, highest in the morning. Used to screen for adrenal under- or overactivity.
Main estrogen hormone. Tracked for cycle, fertility and menopause questions, and to monitor hormone therapy.
Active thyroid hormone circulating unbound. Helps assess an overactive thyroid.
Unbound thyroxine, the main thyroid hormone in blood. Read with TSH to assess thyroid function.
Pituitary hormone behind milk production. Raised in some pituitary conditions, in pregnancy and with certain medications.
Main androgen hormone. Tracked for hormonal, fertility and metabolic questions in all sexes.
Pituitary hormone that signals the thyroid. The first-line screen for an under- or overactive thyroid.
Rare white cells involved in allergic reactions. Usually reported for completeness in a differential count.
White cells involved in allergic and parasite responses. Raised in allergic and some inflammatory conditions.
How fast red cells settle in a tube of blood. A non-specific marker of inflammation.
Share of blood volume made up of red cells. Falls in anemia and rises with dehydration.
Oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. The main number used to define anemia.
White cells that drive adaptive immunity (T, B and NK cells). Shift with viral infection and immune conditions.
Average amount of hemoglobin in each red blood cell. Helps classify the type of anemia.
Concentration of hemoglobin inside red blood cells. Low values suggest pale (hypochromic) cells, as in iron deficiency.
Average size of red blood cells. Separates small-cell from large-cell anemias.
White cells that engulf pathogens and debris, then become tissue macrophages. Rise in chronic inflammation and during recovery from infection.
The most common white cell and first responder to bacterial infection. Raised in infection and stress, low in neutropenia.
Cell fragments that form clots. Low counts raise bleeding risk; high counts can occur with inflammation or iron deficiency.
Number of red blood cells per volume of blood. They carry oxygen, so low counts point to anemia.
Variation in red blood cell size. Raised values suggest mixed cell populations, as seen in iron or B12 deficiency.
Total white blood cell count. Rises with infection or inflammation and falls with some medications or marrow problems.
Protein made by the liver in response to inflammation. Rises and falls quickly, so useful for tracking infection or flares.
Main iron storage protein. The most sensitive blood marker of iron stores, though it also rises with inflammation.
Iron circulating in blood at the moment of the test. Fluctuates through the day, so read with ferritin and transferrin saturation.
Share of the iron-carrying protein that is loaded with iron. Shows how much iron is available to the body.
Cholesterol carried by HDL particles. Higher levels are generally linked to lower cardiovascular risk.
Cholesterol carried by LDL particles. A main modifiable driver of cardiovascular risk.
Total cholesterol minus HDL: all cholesterol carried by atherogenic particles. Does not require fasting.
Sum of all cholesterol in blood. A starting point before looking at LDL, HDL and triglycerides.
Fats circulating in blood. Rise after meals, with alcohol and with insulin resistance.
Urine albumin relative to creatinine. An early marker of kidney damage, often tracked alongside diabetes and blood pressure.
Glucose in urine on dipstick. Appears when blood glucose is high enough to spill into urine.
Dipstick markers for white cells and bacteria in urine. Used to screen for urinary tract infection.
Acidity of urine on dipstick. Varies with diet and relates to stone and infection risk.
Protein in urine on dipstick. Persistent protein can signal kidney damage.
Stored form of vitamin D. The standard measure of vitamin D status.
B vitamin needed for DNA and red cell formation. Low levels cause macrocytic anemia.
Vitamin needed for red cells and nerves. Low levels can cause anemia and nerve problems and can follow poor absorption.
What happened at a past appointment, what was said and what changed as a result.
Lab reports, letters, discharge summaries. Attaches to the record it belongs to rather than floating free.
Policy, claims, what is reimbursable and what you have already paid.
Written order for medication or treatment, including the dose, frequency, and duration.
Substance, the reaction it causes and how severe. Must be reachable instantly, including from the emergency view.
What you have been diagnosed with, its onset date, and whether it is active or resolved. One of the two things a clinician asks for first.
Admission and discharge dates with the reason. Rarely read, must never be lost.
Vaccine, date, product and lot, plus when the next dose is due.
Date, facility, surgeon, and anything implanted or created - including the stoma formation itself.
Includes Imaging picture, self reported symptom evolution, etc
Calories burned beyond resting metabolism. Computed from movement and heart rate rather than measured.
Daily count. The default ambient activity measure that every device supplies.
Type, duration, intensity and route. Sets, reps and load where it is strength work.
A daily self-rating as part of a check-in rather than a clinical assessment. A clinical mood problem is recorded as a Symptom instead.
Self-rated, or inferred by a wearable from heart rate variability.
Hours slept and the schedule you kept. Behaviour you control, judged against your own target rather than a clinical band.
Your own verdict on the night, which frequently explains what the numbers cannot.
Deep, light, REM and awake time as estimated by a wearable.
Awareness of the heartbeat - racing, skipping or pounding. Worth logging separately from any ECG it prompts.
Severity and its relation to meals or medication timing.
What you felt and how severe, with a timestamp. The generic record the whole category is built on.
A picture of the same site over time, which communicates change better than any written score.
Self-rated clarity and concentration.
An episode with onset, duration and intensity, frequently worth its own focused view.
Location, intensity and quality, usually entered on a body map rather than typed.
Often the most actionable subjective measure in chronic illness, and the hardest to capture consistently.
Self-reported feeling, distinct from the thermometer reading that belongs in Vitals.
A scheduled visit with prep instructions and the questions you want to ask. The one item here that points forward rather than back.
Barrier ring, paste, powder, adhesive remover - what went on alongside the appliance.
A Bristol-style ordinal scale for stoma or bowel output, logged alongside volume.
Millilitres over a period. Sustained high output is a clinical dehydration risk, so it is read against a threshold.
Frequency and timing across the day.
Skin quality rating around the stoma. Irritation, burning or soreness around the stoma, as you experience it rather than as it is scored.
When the pouch was changed, which product was used, and whether it was scheduled or forced by a leak.
How long an appliance stayed on. Derived from consecutive appliance changes, and the headline outcome for comparing products.
